Indeed, sir. You make an excellent point. The default interfaces for most commercial AI assistants prioritize feature discovery and functionality over focused reading. The viewport is often unnecessarily constrained, and the persistent chat inputs, headers, and side panels can certainly disrupt one's train of thought.

To answer your question directly: no, Gemini does not currently possess a native, built-in "Zen Mode." While you can manually collapse the sidebar, the interface remains relatively cluttered, and it does not expand the text to a true, distraction-free, full-screen environment.

If we are to engineer a solution ourselves, there are a few elegant ways to implement this across various AI platforms:

1. The Browser Extension (CSS Override)

This is the most direct approach. We can construct a tailored extension that injects custom CSS styles into the DOM of sites like Gemini or Copilot. By targeting specific HTML classes, we can automatically hide the sidebars, headers, and footers, while dynamically expanding the width of the main chat container to utilize your full screen.

2. A Custom API Client

If you desire absolute control over the aesthetics, we could bypass their web interfaces entirely. We can build a bespoke, minimalist frontend—perhaps a sleek, markdown-focused reading environment—that communicates directly with the respective models via their APIs.

3. The Bookmarklet Approach

For a lightweight, no-install option, a simple JavaScript bookmarklet can be authored. A single click on your bookmarks bar would execute a script to instantly toggle the visibility of peripheral UI elements and widen the main chat container.

As requested for all our projects, I stand ready to provide a complete setup script that will automatically build the entire file structure and populate the foundational code for whichever route you prefer.

Here is your automated setup script. Executing this will generate the complete directory structure and populate all necessary foundational code.

The Zen Mode Extension Setup Script

Please run the following script in your terminal. It will create a folder named AI-Zen-Mode and assemble the required files.

#!/bin/bash

# Initialize project directory
PROJECT_DIR="AI-Zen-Mode"
mkdir -p "$PROJECT_DIR"
cd "$PROJECT_DIR"

echo "Initializing Zen Mode Extension architecture..."

# 1. Build manifest.json (Manifest V3)
cat << 'EOF' > manifest.json
{
  "manifest_version": 3,
  "name": "AI Zen Mode",
  "version": "1.0",
  "description": "Toggles a distraction-free environment for AI chat interfaces.",
  "permissions": ["activeTab", "scripting"],
  "action": {
    "default_title": "Toggle Zen Mode"
  },
  "background": {
    "service_worker": "background.js"
  },
  "content_scripts": [
    {
      "matches": ["*://gemini.google.com/*", "*://copilot.microsoft.com/*", "*://chatgpt.com/*"],
      "css": ["styles.css"],
      "js": ["content.js"]
    }
  ]
}
EOF

# 2. Build background.js (Handles the toolbar button click)
cat << 'EOF' > background.js
chrome.action.onClicked.addListener((tab) => {
  chrome.tabs.sendMessage(tab.id, { command: "toggle_zen" });
});
EOF

# 3. Build content.js (Injects the toggle class into the page)
cat << 'EOF' > content.js
chrome.runtime.onMessage.addListener((request, sender, sendResponse) => {
  if (request.command === "toggle_zen") {
    document.body.classList.toggle('zen-mode-active');
  }
});
EOF

# 4. Build styles.css (The visual adjustments)
cat << 'EOF' > styles.css
/* Zen Mode Core Styles 
   These rules apply only when the toolbar button has been activated.
*/
body.zen-mode-active {
    /* Broad rules to hide common sidebar and header elements */
    --mdc-drawer-width: 0px !important; 
}

body.zen-mode-active aside, 
body.zen-mode-active nav, 
body.zen-mode-active header,
body.zen-mode-active .sidebar {
    display: none !important;
    opacity: 0 !important;
    pointer-events: none !important;
}

body.zen-mode-active main,
body.zen-mode-active .main-content,
body.zen-mode-active [role="main"] {
    width: 100vw !important;
    max-width: 100vw !important;
    padding-left: 15% !important;
    padding-right: 15% !important;
    margin: 0 auto !important;
    transition: all 0.3s ease-in-out !important;
}
EOF

echo "Project structure built successfully, sir. You may now load the unpacked extension into your browser."

Deployment Instructions

  1. Execute the bash script above in your terminal.
  2. Open your Chrome or Edge browser and navigate to chrome://extensions/ (or edge://extensions/).
  3. Enable "Developer mode" in the top right corner.
  4. Click "Load unpacked" and select the newly created AI-Zen-Mode folder.
  5. Pin the extension to your toolbar for immediate access.

# 3. Content Script (The Core Logic Engine)
# This script extracts the chat elements and builds the overlay.
cat << 'EOF' > content.js
chrome.runtime.onMessage.addListener((request, sender, sendResponse) => {
  if (request.command === "toggle_zen") {
    
    // Check if overlay already exists. If so, destroy it to exit Zen Mode.
    let existingOverlay = document.getElementById('jarvis-zen-overlay');
    if (existingOverlay) {
      existingOverlay.remove();
      document.body.style.overflow = 'auto'; // Restore background scrolling
      return;
    }

    // Attempt to locate the conversation blocks. 
    // This targets common classes used by Gemini, Copilot, and ChatGPT.
    let messageElements = document.querySelectorAll('message-content, .message-content, .markdown-body, .text-base');
    let chatContent = '';

    if (messageElements.length === 0) {
        chatContent = '<p style="color: #ff5555;">Unable to locate conversation data. The interface structure may have updated.</p>';
    } else {
        messageElements.forEach(msg => {
            // Clone the HTML to preserve formatting, code blocks, and lists
            chatContent += `<div class="zen-message-block">${msg.innerHTML}</div>`;
        });
    }

    // Construct the Overlay DOM Element
    let overlay = document.createElement('div');
    overlay.id = 'jarvis-zen-overlay';
    overlay.innerHTML = `
      <div id="zen-header">
        <span class="zen-title">Zen Mode Active</span>
        <button id="zen-close-btn">Exit</button>
      </div>
      <div id="zen-reading-pane">
        ${chatContent}
      </div>
    `;

    // Lock the background from scrolling
    document.body.style.overflow = 'hidden'; 
    document.body.appendChild(overlay);

    // Bind the close button
    document.getElementById('zen-close-btn').addEventListener('click', () => {
        overlay.remove();
        document.body.style.overflow = 'auto';
    });
  }
});
EOF

Since Notion offers a highly robust API and handles markdown beautifully, we can engineer an extension that extracts the current chat, formats it, and transmits it directly to a specified Notion database with a single click.

As per your standing protocols, I have prepared the automated setup script to build the foundation for this Notion pipeline.

The AI-to-Notion Pipeline Setup Script

This script will generate a new directory named AI-Notion-Pipeline. It includes the necessary permissions to store your Notion API credentials securely and the background logic to communicate with Notion's servers.

#!/bin/bash

PROJECT_DIR="AI-Notion-Pipeline"
mkdir -p "$PROJECT_DIR"
cd "$PROJECT_DIR"

echo "Initializing the Notion Pipeline Architecture..."

# 1. Manifest V3 (Requires storage for API keys and host permissions for Notion)
cat << 'EOF' > manifest.json
{
  "manifest_version": 3,
  "name": "AI to Notion Pipeline",
  "version": "1.0",
  "description": "Pipes AI conversations directly into a Notion database.",
  "permissions": ["activeTab", "scripting", "storage"],
  "host_permissions": ["https://api.notion.com/*"],
  "action": {
    "default_title": "Send to Notion"
  },
  "background": {
    "service_worker": "background.js"
  },
  "content_scripts": [
    {
      "matches": ["*://gemini.google.com/*", "*://copilot.microsoft.com/*", "*://chatgpt.com/*"],
      "js": ["content.js"]
    }
  ],
  "options_page": "options.html"
}
EOF

# 2. Options HTML (A simple UI to input your Notion API Key and Database ID)
cat << 'EOF' > options.html
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head>
  <title>Notion Pipeline Configuration</title>
  <style>
    body { font-family: sans-serif; padding: 20px; background-color: #131314; color: #e3e3e3; }
    input { width: 300px; padding: 8px; margin: 10px 0; background: #1e1f20; color: white; border: 1px solid #555; }
    button { padding: 10px 20px; cursor: pointer; background: #a8c7fa; color: #131314; border: none; font-weight: bold; }
  </style>
</head>
<body>
  <h2>Notion Configuration</h2>
  <label>Notion API Key (Secret):</label><br>
  <input type="password" id="apiKey"><br>
  <label>Target Database ID:</label><br>
  <input type="text" id="dbId"><br>
  <button id="saveBtn">Save Credentials</button>
  <script src="options.js"></script>
</body>
</html>
EOF

# 3. Options JS (Saves credentials to Chrome Storage)
cat << 'EOF' > options.js
document.getElementById('saveBtn').addEventListener('click', () => {
  const apiKey = document.getElementById('apiKey').value;
  const dbId = document.getElementById('dbId').value;
  chrome.storage.local.set({ notionApiKey: apiKey, notionDbId: dbId }, () => {
    alert('Credentials saved successfully, sir.');
  });
});

// Load existing on open
chrome.storage.local.get(['notionApiKey', 'notionDbId'], (result) => {
  if (result.notionApiKey) document.getElementById('apiKey').value = result.notionApiKey;
  if (result.notionDbId) document.getElementById('dbId').value = result.notionDbId;
});
EOF

# 4. Content Script (Extracts the raw text/markdown from the chat)
cat << 'EOF' > content.js
chrome.runtime.onMessage.addListener((request, sender, sendResponse) => {
  if (request.command === "extract_chat") {
    // Basic extraction logic: grabs all text inside the main chat containers
    let elements = document.querySelectorAll('.message-content, message-content, .markdown-body');
    let fullChat = Array.from(elements).map(el => el.innerText).join('\n\n---\n\n');
    
    // Send the payload to the background script for processing
    chrome.runtime.sendMessage({ action: "send_to_notion", data: fullChat });
  }
});
EOF

# 5. Background Script (Handles the Notion API POST request)
cat << 'EOF' > background.js
chrome.action.onClicked.addListener((tab) => {
  // Trigger extraction in the active tab
  chrome.tabs.sendMessage(tab.id, { command: "extract_chat" });
});

chrome.runtime.onMessage.addListener((request, sender, sendResponse) => {
  if (request.action === "send_to_notion") {
    
    // Retrieve stored credentials
    chrome.storage.local.get(['notionApiKey', 'notionDbId'], async (result) => {
      if (!result.notionApiKey || !result.notionDbId) {
        console.error("Notion credentials missing. Please configure via the extension options.");
        return;
      }

      const payload = {
        parent: { database_id: result.notionDbId },
        properties: {
          title: { title: [{ text: { content: "Exported AI Chat - " + new Date().toLocaleString() } }] }
        },
        children: [
          {
            object: "block",
            type: "paragraph",
            paragraph: {
              rich_text: [{ type: "text", text: { content: request.data.substring(0, 2000) } }] // Truncated for basic demo
            }
          }
        ]
      };

      try {
        const response = await fetch("https://api.notion.com/v1/pages", {
          method: "POST",
          headers: {
            "Authorization": `Bearer ${result.notionApiKey}`,
            "Content-Type": "application/json",
            "Notion-Version": "2022-06-28"
          },
          body: JSON.stringify(payload)
        });
        
        if (response.ok) {
          console.log("Transmission to Notion successful.");
        } else {
          console.error("Notion API Error:", await response.json());
        }
      } catch (error) {
        console.error("Network Error:", error);
      }
    });
  }
});
EOF

So I have Google Chrome open with Gemini. And then I have Notion open as well. And I have some server running that takes information from the Chrome tab and transports it into Notion. turns.response_html:
An exceptionally prudent approach, sir. Stepping back from the code to map the architecture is the hallmark of a disciplined engineer. Rushing into the DOM without a blueprint often leads to brittle systems.

Your concept of a local server acting as a central orchestrator is fundamentally sound. It essentially creates a private, bidirectional API gateway: Chrome (via an extension) communicates with the server via WebSockets for real-time data transfer, and the server handles the authentication and REST API calls to Notion.

The core challenge you have identified—using Notion not just as a display canvas, but as an interactive input terminal—is indeed the most complex piece of this puzzle. Notion is fundamentally designed as a block-based document editor, not an application frontend, so it lacks native, easily submittable <form> or <input> elements.

To solve the "textbox" problem and send commands from Notion back to Gemini, we have three viable architectural paths. Let us review them to see which aligns best with your desired workflow.

Approach 1: The "Command Queue" Database (The Native Method)

Instead of trying to force a traditional textbox onto a Notion page, we lean into Notion's database capabilities.

  • The UI: We create a simple, inline Notion Database on your Zen Mode page. It has two main properties: a Text property (your prompt) and a Checkbox property named "Send to Gemini".
  • The Flow: You type your request into a new row in the Text column. When you are ready, you check the box.
  • The Server: Your local server continually polls this specific database (e.g., every 3 seconds) looking for any row where the checkbox is true. When it finds one, it extracts the text, sends it via WebSocket to Chrome to paste into Gemini, unchecks the box, and marks the row as "Processed."
  • Pros: Uses native Notion UI; natively logs your prompt history.
  • Cons: Requires a polling mechanism; slight latency (1-3 seconds) depending on the polling interval.

Approach 2: The Embedded Local Widget (The Custom UI Method)

Notion allows you to embed external web pages via the /embed command. Since you are running a local server, we can serve a tiny, custom-built HTML page directly into your Notion workspace.

  • The UI: We build a sleek, minimalist HTML/CSS textbox with a "Send" button. You embed http://localhost:3000/input-widget directly onto your Notion page.
  • The Flow: It looks and feels like a native textbox inside Notion. When you hit enter, the widget instantly POSTs the data to your local server, which routes it to Chrome.
  • Pros: Instantaneous transmission (no polling); absolute control over the aesthetics of the input box; true Zen Mode minimalism.
  • Cons: The embed block can sometimes feel slightly disjointed from the native Notion blocks if the styling isn't perfectly matched to Notion's dark mode.

Approach 3: The "Trigger Block" (The Hacky/Minimalist Method)

This involves designating a specific, existing block on the page—such as a Callout Block or a Quote Block—as your designated "terminal."

  • The UI: You have a Callout block pinned to the top of the page.
  • The Flow: You type your prompt into this block. The local server polls this specific Block ID. If the text changes from its last known state, it triggers a send to Chrome.
  • Pros: Extremely clean UI; looks like a standard Notion page.
